headline: Total Wine urges customers to fight 11 December hemp THC ban
dek: With 15 days left before the federal 0.4 mg THC cap, Total Wine & More and South Carolina hemp drink makers are pressing Congress for rules instead of a ban.
key_points: Total Wine & More is asking customers to contact members of Congress before the federal hemp definition changes on 11 December, calling low-dose THC drinks its fastest-growing category.
Its government affairs chief, Eric Brewer, proposed regulating THC drinks like alcohol, with a three-tier system and US-grown products.
In South Carolina, beverage makers and a hemp shop owner said the change threatens their businesses, and State Sen. Deon Tedder wrote to Congress seeking a block or a delay.
Many products now on shelves carry up to 10 mg of THC; the federal cap from 11 December is 0.4 mg per container, one twenty-fifth of that.
body: The fight over the 11 December hemp deadline now has one of America's largest alcohol retailers in it. Total Wine & More is urging its customers to contact their members of Congress about the federal change that will cap hemp-derived THC at 0.4 milligrams per container, KTTC in Rochester, Minnesota, reported on 24 November. The retailer said low-dose THC drinks are its fastest-growing category.

In South Carolina, hemp beverage makers and shop owners told WCSC, in a report carried by WTOC on 25 November, that they are bracing for the change, and a state senator has written to Congress asking it to step in. The pressure comes from the same retail and beverage businesses that grew up around the 2018 Farm Bill, and it runs straight into Senate Republicans who want the ban to stand.
## Total Wine's pitch: regulate it like alcohol

Eric Brewer, Total Wine's senior vice president of government relations and public affairs, told KTTC that demand for low-dose THC drinks is high and that the wider THC products market is worth roughly $30 billion, a figure he gave without a source. His proposal is to regulate the products rather than remove them: require them to be made from US-grown hemp and sell them through a three-tier system like the one used for alcohol, with separate production, wholesale and retail tiers.

Brewer argued that nearly all of the concern in Washington is about high-dose and non-beverage products, not the drinks his stores sell. Prohibition, he said, would push demand into unregulated channels. His message to lawmakers was blunt: "Congress needs to choose regulation, not prohibition."

That is a notable shift in who is speaking for hemp. Until now the loudest voices against the 11 December change have been hemp growers, CBD companies, craft brewers and veterans' groups. A national alcohol chain arguing for a three-tier THC system brings the distribution model of the drinks industry directly into the debate.
> The hemp fight is no longer just hemp versus marijuana. Alcohol retail now has a stake in what happens on 11 December.

In Charleston, the WCSC report spoke to beverage and retail businesses that depend on hemp THC sales. They included Ty Gilmore, president of Reframe Beverages, and Justin Buchanan, a co-owner of the Charleston-based company; Matt Skinner, chief executive of High Rise Beverage; and Libis Skinner, owner of Charleston Hemp Collective. They described the coming change as a threat to their businesses, and the report said some hemp jobs could disappear.

State Sen. Deon Tedder has sent a letter to Congress urging lawmakers to block the restrictions or delay them long enough to build a regulatory framework, according to the report. The station also cited a claim that South Carolina's hemp industry puts more than $50 billion into the economy; it gave no source for that figure, and we have not been able to verify it.

From 11 December, a finished hemp product with more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container falls outside the federal definition of hemp. The WCSC report noted that many products on shelves today carry up to 10 milligrams of THC and that products relying on other forms of THC, such as delta-8, would also be illegal under the new law. On our arithmetic, a single 10 mg drink holds 25 times the THC the new rule allows in an entire container.

That is why the retailers' argument focuses on regulation rather than a higher cap. No product built around a few milligrams of THC can be reformulated to fit under 0.4 milligrams and still do what customers buy it for.
## The bill they are pointing to

The alternative Total Wine cited is the Hemp Guardrails Act, introduced on 17 November by Sens. Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, and Tim Sheehy, a Montana Republican. According to MPR News, the bill would ban sales of hemp-derived THC products to people under 21 nationwide, create a federal regulatory framework that does not exist today, and give the Food and Drug Administration authority over hemp-derived cannabinoid products and dietary supplements. The Minnesota Craft Brewers Guild has said it supports the bill as written.

The obstacle is the calendar and the Senate. As we reported on 25 November, 14 Republican senators led by Ted Budd wrote to President Trump asking him to let the change take effect and to oppose any delay in the coming spending bill. The White House, meanwhile, has asked Congress only to protect non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD, not THC drinks. Government funding and the hemp change both run out on 11 December, so the spending bill is the most likely vehicle for any fix.

Watch the text of the stopgap spending bill that must pass by 11 December: whether it includes the White House's narrow CBD fix, a broader delay, or nothing on hemp. Watch whether the Hemp Guardrails Act gains co-sponsors or a committee hearing before then. And watch state regulators, who are already telling retailers to clear shelves of over-limit products before the deadline.
